name: Breath (James Nestor) nasal breathing

card.summary: A set of nasal-breathing and mouth-taping practices popularised by James Nestor's 2020 book Breath, which looksmaxxers pair with jaw and face-structure goals.
card.note: Mouth taping is impractical when the nose is blocked; people with sleep apnea or breathing conditions are usually advised to ask a clinician first.

quick.overview:
Breath: The New Science of a Lost Art is a 2020 popular-science book by journalist James Nestor. It argues that many modern people have drifted into habitual mouth breathing and that returning to breathing through the nose supports sleep, health and, in the view of some readers, how the face and jaw look.

In looksmaxxing circles the book is a reference point for nasal breathing, mouth taping at night and related ideas about tongue posture and airway. Proponents link nose breathing to better sleep and recovery and to a forward, well-supported facial structure. Published research on mouth taping is small, and expert commentary on the book's broader claims is mixed.
quick.how: In practice, people try to breathe through the nose during the day, during exercise and during sleep. Some place a strip of gentle tape over the lips at night, and some add tongue-posture habits or slow breathing exercises described in the book. Practitioners usually describe it as a lifestyle habit used alongside other sleep and posture routines.
quick.risks: Mouth taping is not suited to anyone whose nasal passages are blocked by a deviated septum, allergies, sinus problems or congestion, and tape on the face can irritate skin. Clinicians generally want sleep apnea diagnosed and managed properly rather than self-treated. Reviewers of the book have also cautioned that some health claims rest on anecdote.

lead: Breath: The New Science of a Lost Art is a 2020 book by science journalist James Nestor, published by Riverhead Books on 26 May 2020 [1]. It covers the history, science and culture of breathing and argues that many people have moved from nasal breathing to chronic mouth breathing, a shift the book links to snoring, sleep apnea, asthma and allergies [1]. Nestor also describes his own breathing experiments, including time spent with researchers at Stanford University [1].

Within looksmaxxing, the book is cited as a starting point for nasal breathing and for mouth taping, a practice of keeping the lips closed with tape during sleep [2]. Followers connect these habits to better sleep and recovery, which they see as supporting energy, skin and training, and some connect chronic mouth breathing to narrower jaws and a recessed face, an idea shared with mewing and orthotropics communities [3].

The book was an international bestseller, selling more than two million copies by April 2023 [1]. Reviewers praised its readability and also raised concerns: one critic in The Wall Street Journal wrote that it applied too little skepticism and relied on shaky evidence, and another in The Spectator said it leans on anecdote [1]. Research on mouth taping specifically is described as very limited [2].

chain: Breathe through the nose by day and at night
Fewer mouth-breathing nights, more settled sleep
Better rest and recovery; some also expect a better-supported jaw and face
angle.text: Followers use nasal breathing and mouth taping to improve sleep, energy and recovery, which they see as feeding into skin, training and a rested look. A smaller group goes further and expects nasal breathing combined with tongue posture to support a more forward jaw and midface.

paras: Nestor's book is part history, part reportage and part memoir of experiments. It argues that humans have lost breathing skills, partly because of processed foods and modern living, and that mouth breathing is associated with snoring, sleep apnea, asthma, autoimmune disease and allergies [1]. The book recounts experiments in which Nestor worked with Stanford scientists on the effects of returning to nasal breathing [1].
Breathing through the nose filters, warms and humidifies air, and proponents also point to nitric oxide produced in the nasal passages, which advocates say may aid blood flow and blood pressure [2].

Looksmaxxing communities treat the book as a reference for the nasal-breathing side of facial development. The idea they discuss is that chronic mouth breathing during growth is tied to a long, narrow face, while nose breathing with the tongue resting on the palate is tied to a broader, more forward jaw [3]. The same communities discuss mewing, the tongue-posture practice named after orthodontist John Mew [3].

Mouth taping is the most visible practice that spread from the book's themes. It means holding the lips closed with a strip of tape during sleep so that breathing happens through the nose [2]. Social media popularised it in the 2020s [2].

Research on mouth taping is very limited. A 2022 preliminary study reported a lower apnea-hypopnea index in mild-apnea mouth breathers who taped, and a 2015 pilot study using porous oral patches reported a similar reduction; both observed less snoring [2].
Mouth breathing during sleep can dry the mouth, which is linked to dental problems, bad breath, hoarseness and dry lips, and taping is impractical for people whose nasal breathing is obstructed [2].

On the face-shape claims, no credible scientific research has demonstrated that orthotropics, the tongue-posture practice John Mew promoted, reshapes the jaws, and the American Association of Orthodontists has reported no evidence that it improves the jaw [3]. Reviewers of the book itself have said its health claims lean on anecdote and that its descriptions of nitric oxide and carbon dioxide effects are vague [1].

No published trial has tested the book's overall protocol for appearance. Small studies of mouth taping and oral patches in people with mild sleep apnea reported reduced apnea severity and snoring [2].

lore.intro: Online, Breath is treated as the source text for nose breathing and mouth taping, often alongside mewing and jaw-development discussions [1][3].

claims.claim: Nasal breathing and tongue posture give a better jaw and face
claims.believers: Proponents say that nose breathing keeps the tongue up and supports forward jaw growth, while mouth breathing is tied to a narrow, recessed face [3].
claims.experts: No credible scientific research has shown that orthotropics reshapes the jaws, and the American Association of Orthodontists reports no evidence of jaw improvement [3].

claims.believers: Users say taping encourages nasal breathing, a calmer night and less snoring [2].
claims.experts: Two small studies, in 2022 and 2015, reported lower apnea severity and less snoring in mild apnea, and overall research is described as very limited [2].

claims.claim: Mouth breathing is behind many modern health problems
claims.believers: The book links chronic mouth breathing to snoring, sleep apnea, asthma and allergies [1].
claims.experts: Reviewers wrote that the book overstates health benefits and leans on anecdote [1].
